chapters.observation: Melos and Nuer feud establish the core distinction among emotion, action, organisation, and scale.
Jebel Sahaba's healed and unhealed wounds are contrasted with Nataruk's less secure single-event reconstruction.
The Stele of the Vultures supplies an explicit state narrative of war, while Mohenjo-daro demonstrates the danger of inferring massacre from scattered remains.
Behistun's classification of rebels is compared with Assyrian deportation as two methods of managing imperial difference.
Cajamarca's rapid seizure of Atahualpa is differentiated from the alliance-dependent siege and fall of Tenochtitlan.
Norman dynastic conquest and crusader sacred conquest are compared through oaths, logistics, massacre, and the institutions that followed victory.
The Secret History traces Temujin's rule through rewarded loyalty and redistribution, while Novgorod shows conquest settling into census and tribute.
The Code Noir, Codrington estates, Zong litigation, and Equiano show slavery reproduced through linked legal, religious, commercial, and maritime offices.
The devşirme's regulated extraction of boys is contrasted with Magdeburg's catastrophic extraction of urban goods by an underpaid army.
The October Days retain negotiable political demands, whereas the September prison killings target people already stripped of leverage.
Congo rubber quotas and German East African cotton policy depend on local intermediaries who make distant colonial demands enforceable.
Somme logistics and Armenian deportation orders use similar administrative capacities toward radically different selected targets.
Wannsee's interoffice coordination is placed beside Sonderkommando photographs and testimony from inside the killing system.
Cuban missile correspondence shows restraint through signalling, while the Briggs Plan reorganises civilian settlement, food, and information.
Taiping demographic uncertainty is compared with abolitionist evidence-making to define what records can establish and what remains unknowable.
